properties.description:
THE LESSON: a capability can be built, verified, documented and used by nobody, and every signal in the design will read green.

`cap:publish-surface` was VERIFIED. `req:publishable-promise` was ACCEPTED — "a published surface must be able to carry a behavioural promise, not only structure". `set_requirement_designation` shipped and works. And reflow2 published 0 of its 262 requirements, for months, while a real consumer mirrored it correctly and received 22 nodes of pure structure.

⭐ THE SYMPTOM ARRIVED AS A HUMAN COMPLAINT, NOT AS A FINDING. Anthony: flo2's sessions keep needing to be reminded they can read reflow2's design. flo2's own graph already held a root-cause record for that from three days earlier, which named it the THIRD occurrence and closed with "there is no test that fails today for any of this — an agent did not look has no executable form — so this is a CONTAINMENT, not a cure." True of THAT cause. It hid a second one underneath: there was nothing in the mirror worth looking at.

⇒ AN AGENT THAT STOPS MENTIONING A RESOURCE WHICH NEVER ANSWERS ANYTHING IS BEHAVING SENSIBLY. The repair was not to the agent.

WHAT LANDED: `published_surface_carries_no_intent`, and six requirements marked `published` on Anthony's word — chosen for what flo2 actually relies on: many designs on one service, the trust boundary at ingress, the read-only hosted surface, a refusal naming what would have worked, conventions riding the tool, and a design reachable without the repo.

AND THE DISCIPLINE THAT SHAPED THE CHOICE: four of the first six candidates were still `proposed`. Publishing a proposed requirement would promise a consumer something the owner has not settled, so the set was narrowed to accepted ones. `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` is why an agent may not simply accept them to make the list nicer.
properties.name: The published surface gains its first promises, and something finally notices when it has none
